clue.text: Carnivore's circle at Fast (reported in Powys)

definitions.note: a title told of by the novelist John Cowper Powys, i.e. one of his novels

explanation.surface: A predator's ring sits by a fast, as some account from the Welsh county of Powys tells it.
explanation.walkthrough: Powys looks like the Welsh county, but here it is the novelist John Cowper Powys, whose 1929 novel this is.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cowper Powys wrote a novel with this title about a Dorset schoolmaster.

clue.text: We are told the Ethiopian may not change his skin, nor the leopard these

parts.note: Jeremiah 13:23 asks whether the leopard can change his spots; the clue wants the zoological word for those eye-like spots

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb has the leopard unable to change his spots; the answer is the technical name for eye-shaped markings such as a leopard's rosettes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocellated markings are eye-like spots, the kind on a leopard's coat in the biblical saying.

clue.text: "You can have as much — as you like —— at your Boffins" (Our Mutual Friend)

clue.text: Stravinsky's King of Thebes, the musical

clue.text: He, confused with rich student, was German Nobel prizewinner

indicators.note: confused means the letters of the words beside it are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: L is a learner, the student driver's plate

explanation.surface: A man is muddled with a wealthy pupil, yet he was a German who won a Nobel prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' scrambles HE, RICH and L (student, from the learner plate) together.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Ehrlich, German bacteriologist, shared the 1908 Nobel Prize for medicine for his work on immunity.

explanation.walkthrough: Chateaubriand sounds like the steak, but it is the French writer, whose memoirs appeared posthumously under a title meaning memoirs from beyond the grave.

clue.text: Composer of church music, presumably after Closing Time?

definitions.text: Composer of church music, presumably after Closing Time?

parts.words: Composer of church music, presumably after Closing Time?

explanation.walkthrough: John Taverner was a Tudor composer of masses; read as a common noun the name is an innkeeper, whose work ends at closing time.
explanation.definitionFit: John Taverner wrote masses and motets for the Tudor church; a taverner keeps an inn.

clue.text: Whose holiday? Rowland Lacy's

explanation.walkthrough: In Thomas Dekker's comedy, the nobleman Rowland Lacy disguises himself as a craftsman of the gentle craft, so the holiday is his too.
explanation.definitionFit: Dekker's play is titled after the cobblers' holiday, and Lacy joins that trade in disguise.

clue.text: Ah, Moll looks different for ancient Irish sage

explanation.surface: A woman named Moll appears altered, mistaken for a wise old Irishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looks different' rearranges AH and MOLL.
explanation.definitionFit: In early Ireland the title was given to a master poet or learned man of the highest rank.

clue.text: Rachel, who must have doubted whether her diamond was her best friend

explanation.walkthrough: The line plays on 'diamonds are a girl's best friend': Rachel's Moonstone caused nothing but trouble in Wilkie Collins's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Rachel Verinder inherits the cursed yellow diamond in Collins's The Moonstone.

clue.text: Girl from Murger gets singing role

explanation.definitionFit: The Pacific nation is an archipelago of over three hundred islands.

clue.text: "Armstrong", of Norway, who had the last word

clue.text: Season for which the cherry wore white

definitions.text: Season for which the cherry wore white

parts.note: recalls Housman's poem in which the cherry tree is wearing white blossom for a spring church festival

clue.text: Maugham's bondage girl

clue.text: Like Naomi Mitchison's eponymous losers?
